claims.text: The high-entropy alloy has local lattice distortions arising from atomic-size mismatches among its principal elements.
Atomic-size mismatch is significant in the proposed as-fabricated high-entropy alloy.
Lattice distortions create local stress fields.
The local stress fields produced by lattice distortions interact with mobile dislocations during deformation.
Interactions between distortion-induced stress fields and dislocations increase opportunities for dislocation cross-slip.
Interactions between distortion-induced stress fields and dislocations promote dislocation entanglement.
Increased cross-slip and dislocation entanglement produce enhanced dynamic strain hardening.
Enhanced dynamic strain hardening helps maintain both strength and ductility during deformation.
Compared with a conventional binary or ternary baseline having lower lattice distortion, the high-entropy alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate under comparable loading conditions.
Compared with the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will sustain higher ductility under comparable loading conditions.
In situ microscopy or diffraction will reveal more frequent dislocation cross-slip events in the high-entropy alloy than in the baseline.
In situ measurements will reveal greater dislocation entanglement in the high-entropy alloy than in the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should dominate at moderate strain rates and temperatures where dislocation motion is active and before twinning or dynamic recrystallization becomes prevalent.
The relative contribution of lattice distortion, nanotwinning, and transformation-induced plasticity varies with composition and testing conditions.
